sections.h2: How does Florida protect a homestead from creditors?
sections.html:
Article X, section 4 of the Florida Constitution shields a natural person's homestead from forced sale under court process, so no judgment, decree or execution becomes a lien on it. The shield has three carve-outs: taxes and assessments, debts incurred to buy, improve or repair the property, and debts for labor performed on the realty (Florida Constitution, Art. X, s. 4).

The size limit depends on location. Outside a municipality the protected homestead may reach 160 contiguous acres. Inside one, it is one-half acre of contiguous land, and the protection is limited to the residence of the owner or the owner's family. Personal property up to $1,000 gets the same shield, and the protection passes to a surviving spouse or heirs.

sections.h2: Can a Florida homestead be left to anyone in a will?
sections.html:
Not when the owner leaves a spouse or a minor child. The Constitution bars a devise in that case, with one exception: the homestead may go to the spouse if there is no minor child. Section 732.4015 repeats the rule (Florida Statutes, s. 732.4015).

Trusts do not sidestep it. The statute defines "devise" to include a trust disposition of the part of the trust estate that would be homestead if titled in the grantor's name, and it treats the grantor of a qualifying trust as the owner. If a spouse's devised interest is disclaimed, it passes under chapter 739.

For heirs preparing to sell, the practical point is that a will may not control who holds title. The closing agent will ask who survived the owner before it insures a sale.

sections.h2: Who owns the house when the owner dies without a valid devise?
sections.html:
It descends as ordinary intestate property, with a twist for spouses. If the owner left a spouse and descendants, the spouse takes a life estate and the descendants take a vested remainder. Section 732.401 lets the spouse swap that for an undivided one-half interest as a tenant in common, with the other half vesting in the descendants.

The swap has strict mechanics, all from the statute (Florida Statutes, s. 732.401):

  • The election must be made within 6 months after death and during the spouse's lifetime.
  • An attorney in fact or guardian needs court approval, and the petition must also be filed within the 6 months.
  • Once made, the election is irrevocable.
  • It is made by recording a notice of election, with the legal description, in the county's official records.

Until the election is made or the window closes, a buyer cannot be sure what interest the spouse holds. Sellers in this position should bring the recorded notice, or proof none was filed, to the title company early.

sections.h2: Does a married owner need a spouse's signature to sell?
sections.html:
Yes. The Constitution says the owner of homestead real estate, joined by the spouse if married, may alienate the homestead by mortgage, sale or gift. A deed signed by one spouse alone leaves a gap that a title insurer will flag.

The same sentence lets a married owner deed the property into a tenancy by the entirety with the spouse. If the owner or spouse is incompetent, the method of alienation follows what the law provides, which usually means a court or guardian is involved.

Conveyances of land also need to be in writing and signed before two subscribing witnesses under s. 689.01. Have the closing agent review the witness blocks.

sections.h2: What does a spouse's waiver actually waive?
sections.html:
Less than many people assume. Section 732.7025 supplies deed language by which a spouse gives up the devise restriction, allowing the owner to leave the home to someone other than that spouse. Language "substantially similar" to the statute's wording is enough.

The statute then draws two lines (Florida Statutes, s. 732.7025). That waiver does not give up protection against the owner's creditors during life or after death. It also does not remove the restriction on selling, mortgaging or gifting the homestead without the spouse's joinder.

A broader waiver exists in s. 732.702. A surviving spouse's rights to homestead, elective share, intestate share, family allowance and more may be waived by a written agreement signed in front of two subscribing witnesses. Waivers made after marriage require fair disclosure of the signer's estate. A waiver of "all rights" in a property settlement reaches homestead unless it says otherwise (Florida Statutes, s. 732.702).

sections.h2: How do the two waiver statutes compare?
sections.html:
They do different jobs, and sellers often mix them up. This table sets them side by side.

Features. 732.7025 deed waivers. 732.702 written waiver
Where it appearsIn a deedStand-alone contract, agreement or waiver
ScopeDevise restriction onlyHomestead and other spousal rights, wholly or partly
WitnessesStatute prescribes the deed languageTwo subscribing witnesses
Effect on joinder to sellNone, joinder still requiredDepends on the waiver's terms

Source: the two statute pages linked above. A lawyer should draft or review either one.

sections.h2: How does a Florida homestead affect a sale after probate or divorce?
sections.html:
Both events can change who must sign. After a death, check whether the homestead passed by intestacy, whether a spouse made the six-month election, and whether the estate needs administration. Summary administration is available when the non-exempt estate does not exceed $150,000 or the decedent has been dead more than two years (s. 735.201). Creditor claims are barred after the later of three months from first publication of the notice to creditors or 30 days after service on a creditor who must be served (s. 733.702).

Divorce is a separate path. The Constitution's joinder rule still applies to any sale made before the court rules on the marital home, so a buyer's title agent will want the final judgment or the spouse's signature.

Documentary stamp tax rules also apply. The Department of Revenue lists a personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable, and divorce deeds for the marital home and spousal homestead deeds where the only consideration is a mortgage are exempt under s. 201.02(7) (Department of Revenue, documentary stamp tax).

sections.h2: What should an heir or seller gather for a homestead closing?
sections.html:
Title work on a homestead depends on documents showing who held title and who survived. Collect them before the contract goes out.

  • The death certificate and the deed that put the owner on title.
  • Any will or trust instrument, since a trust counts as a devise for homestead purposes.
  • A recorded notice of election if a spouse chose the one-half interest.
  • Any marital agreement or waiver signed before two subscribing witnesses.
  • Divorce judgments that award the marital home.

The constitutional protection also runs to heirs. It inures to the surviving spouse or heirs of the owner, so creditors of the deceased owner face the same limits that applied during life, apart from the listed exceptions for taxes, purchase and improvement debts, and labor on the property.

A short call to the clerk of the circuit court clarifies how recorded documents will appear in the official records, and the clerk's recording charges are set by s. 28.24.

faqs.q: Is a Florida homestead safe from judgment creditors?
faqs.a: Generally yes. A court judgment cannot become a lien on it, but taxes, purchase or improvement debts and labor on the property are exceptions. The shield covers up to 160 acres outside a municipality or one-half acre inside one.

faqs.q: Can I leave my Florida homestead to my children if I am married?
faqs.a: Not by will or trust devise. If a spouse survives you, the homestead cannot be devised to someone else unless the spouse waived that restriction. A devise to the spouse is allowed only if no minor child survives.

faqs.q: Does my wife or husband have to sign the deed to sell?
faqs.a: Yes, on a homestead. The Constitution has the owner joined by the spouse when selling, mortgaging or gifting. Skipping the spouse leaves the deed open to challenge.

faqs.q: How long does a surviving spouse have to elect a half interest?
faqs.a: Six months from the date of death, and the election must be made during the spouse's lifetime. It is irrevocable and made by recording a notice of election with the clerk of that county.

faqs.q: Does the deed waiver language let me sell without my spouse?
faqs.a: No. Section 732.7025 waives only the devise restriction. It does not waive creditor protection or the requirement that a spouse join in any sale, mortgage or gift.
